description: We are a team of two with engineering background.
summary: SteadFast is a heads-up helmet display for astronauts walking on Mars. Because a radio signal takes up to 22 minutes to reach Earth, a question and its answer can take 40 minutes, so an astronaut outside the habitat has to make navigation decisions alone. SteadFast keeps three answers in the line of sight: which way to go, how much margin is left, and when to turn back. Before the walk, the astronaut sets the rules of the route, such as avoiding steep ground or carrying a load, and sees what each rule costs in distance and oxygen. During the walk, the display checks the plan every second. When the walk deviates from the plan, it drops a station, recalculates a safe route from where the astronaut stands, and reports what changed. When radiation rises as it did in a solar particle storm that Curiosity measured, it sends the astronaut back to the habitat. Everything is built on real NASA data from Gale Crater, including orbital terrain, Curiosity's images, radiation readings and rock chemistry, and the oxygen model draws on NASA suit tests and Apollo records. SteadFast is a browser simulation of what the wearer would see, with its limitations labeled.
details:
In short

  • The problem: Communication delays between Earth and Mars take up to 40 minutes, meaning astronauts on an extravehicular activity (EVA) must make critical navigation decisions alone.
  • What we built: A heads-up helmet display that continuously answers three vital questions: which way to go, how much margin is left, and when to turn back.
  • The core feature: Whenever a walk deviates from the plan, the display immediately recalculates a safe route and tells the astronaut what changed.
  • The foundation: The simulation is built on real NASA data from Gale Crater, cross-checked against field measurements, with model limitations clearly labeled.

1. The problem: walking where no one can answer in time

On Mars, astronauts cannot rely on Mission Control for real-time guidance because communication delays are too long and EVA plans frequently slip.

  • The communication delay: On the date our demo simulates (4 November 2025), a radio signal takes 20 minutes to travel one way, meaning a question and its answer take 40 minutes.
  • Schedules slip: In NASA's review of the Apollo moonwalks, 8 out of 11 EVAs ran longer than planned (Miller et al., 2017).
  • Oxygen runs low: In 9 out of 12 Apollo cases, crew members finished with less oxygen than originally projected.

Because a Mars walker cannot wait 40 minutes for help when conditions change, the suit itself must detect when a plan no longer works and calculate what to do next.

2. The view: three questions answered in the line of sight

First-person view during an automated walk, roughly 120 m into the route. Screenshot from our app using simulated walker movement, clock, and oxygen supply. Partner figure is AI-generated via Tripo.

To keep the astronaut's eyes on the terrain, the interface shows:

  1. Which way to follow? A ribbon with moving arrows projects the route directly onto the ground ahead. This path minimizes oxygen consumption based on the safety rules the astronaut selected before departing.
  2. How much time and oxygen is left? A status line beneath the central gauge displays the remaining margin before the astronaut must turn back. This figure represents the tighter constraint between remaining time and oxygen, after accounting for the return trip and a mandatory 30-minute reserve. When walking in pairs, the system automatically tracks whichever astronaut will run low first.
  3. Is it still safe to continue? A central gauge issues a single, high-visibility directive: GO, CAUTION, HEAD HOME, TURN BACK, or EMERGENCY.

To ensure astronauts can distinguish hard sensor readings from model estimates, every number on screen carries a small icon indicating its source: measured by a NASA mission, modeled from NASA data, computed from geometry, or simulated.

3. Before the walk: the astronaut sets the decisive factors that should be prioritized in route planning

The pre-walk planning screen showing default settings (avoid steep ground, 08:08 departure, 0 kg load). Cyan: active plan. Amber: lowest-oxygen path ignoring slope rules. White dashes: shortest distance. Red: slopes steeper than 24°.

Before stepping outside, the astronaut configures the walk's constraints and immediately sees the resource cost of each choice:

  • Fixed baseline: Oxygen consumption is always factored into every calculation.
  • Customizable rules: The astronaut can choose to treat steep ground as an obstacle, avoid terrain shadows, add a carried load (0 to 30 kg), and select one of three departure hours.
  • How the path is computed: Every time a setting changes, Dijkstra's algorithm searches a 2 m terrain grid to find the lowest-cost path that satisfies all active rules.

Comparing three planning strategies (08:08 departure, no load):

  • Shortest distance: 722 m | 51.5 g of oxygen | crosses 16 m of steep ground.
  • Lowest oxygen only: 733 m | 51.0 g of oxygen | crosses 18 m of steep ground.
  • Active plan (with steep-ground rule): 738 m | 51.4 g of oxygen | 0 m on steep ground.

Why the rule matters: On this short loop, avoiding steep terrain costs only 5 m of extra distance and 0.4 g of oxygen, while eliminating 18 m of hazardous footing. Rather than blocking steep slopes entirely, the planner treats them as a "soft obstacle" with a 10x movement penalty, so the route only crosses slopes steeper than 24° (the upper limit of the slope-energy data from Minetti et al., 2002) when no detour exists. Including scientific work at three stations, the full baseline plan takes about 95 minutes and 157 g of oxygen.

4. During the walk: real-time replanning

Once every second, the display evaluates whether the current plan is still viable. A plan passes only if the remaining stations fit within the available time and oxygen (above the 30-minute reserve) and at least 90% of 1,000 simulated Monte Carlo walks complete it. As soon as a plan fails this check, the system drops a station, reroutes from the astronaut's current position, and reports the change.

Case 1: Running behind schedule

Six hours into the walk. The simulation clock was manually advanced for this frame because this short loop would not run late on its own. Partner figure is AI-generated via Tripo.

  1. At the 6.0-hour mark, visiting Stations B and C plus returning to the habitat requires 106 g of oxygen, but only 99 g remains above the reserve.
  2. Because the current plan is no longer safe, the display automatically drops Station C, keeps Station B, and calculates a new route requiring just 61 g.
  3. The astronaut sees a single, clear alert: "Late. STN C dropped. New route: STN B → HAB."
  4. Half an hour later, as margins tighten further, the system drops Station B as well and switches the main directive to HEAD HOME.

Case 2: A solar particle storm

Replay of the solar particle storm measured by Curiosity on 20 May 2024. Partner figure is AI-generated via Tripo.

  1. The panel displays live radiation dose rates from Curiosity's Radiation Assessment Detector (RAD). During the 20 May 2024 storm, rates surged from 5.6 to 351 µGy/h.
  2. Following a published early-warning rule (Löwe et al., 2025, preprint), the alarm triggers as soon as the dose rate rises 25% above pre-storm baseline levels.
  3. On replayed storm data, this rule triggers the alarm 37 to 53 minutes before peak radiation hits.
  4. Immediately, the central directive switches to TURN BACK, the science route disappears, and a high-priority amber line guides the astronaut along the fastest path back to the habitat.
  5. Because the farthest point on our route is roughly six minutes from the habitat, the astronaut gets inside after receiving no more than about 0.3% of the storm dose that Curiosity's detector recorded.

Other handled scenarios

  • Uneven partner consumption: If one astronaut burns oxygen faster than the other, the system automatically bases the return margin on the faster-consuming partner.
  • Walking off-route: If the astronaut strays more than 10 m off the planned path, the display computes an alternative route in white from their current spot, letting them choose between the new path and the original.
  • Point-of-no-return boundary: Late in the EVA, an amber perimeter line appears on the terrain to show the estimated geographic boundary from which a safe return is still possible.

5. At each station: what Curiosity found

Station A information card. Photo: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS.

Each waypoint corresponds to an actual site investigated by the Curiosity rover. Upon arrival, an information card displays:

  • Site imagery: The actual photo Curiosity captured at that stop.
  • Scientific context: Why the rover team targeted that rock, quoted directly from NASA's image labels.
  • Rock chemistry: Weight percentages (with error ranges) for six oxides measured by Curiosity's APXS and ChemCam instruments.
  • Actionable choices: Three options (complete the planned work, move on, or skip remaining stops and head home), each displaying how much time margin will remain afterward.

(Note: Chemical measurements are provided for scientific context and do not influence route calculations.)

6. NASA data: what drives decisions vs. what provides context

Overview of how different NASA datasets feed into the helmet display.

While the interface displays a wide variety of mission data, only three datasets actively alter navigation and safety decisions. The rest are shown for situational awareness.

Data that drives decisions

  • Orbital terrain (HiRISE / USGS): A 1 m digital elevation model of Gale Crater provides the slope of every grid cell. Because slope dictates walking speed and oxygen burn, it directly shapes the route. Combined with solar position data (JPL Horizons) for the chosen departure hour, this model also calculates terrain shadows.
  • Surface imagery (Curiosity Navcam): Within two 48 m patches, one at the habitat and one at Station A, stereo images map the ground at 5 cm resolution. A computer vision model (DINOv3, fine-tuned on NASA's AI4Mars dataset) classifies each pixel into four terrain types, each applying a multiplier to oxygen cost: bedrock (1.0x), soil (1.2x), big rock (1.5x), and sand (2.1x).
  • Radiation levels (Curiosity RAD): Live dose-rate readings directly control the solar storm alarm.

Terrain classification overlay near the habitat, toggled with the C key. Partner figure is AI-generated via Tripo.

Data shown for context only

  • Air and ground temperatures at the departure hour (REMS)
  • Rock chemistry at each station (APXS, ChemCam)
  • Regional maps (JPL Mars Trek, USGS geology)
  • Real-time Earth-Mars radio delay (JPL Horizons)

How oxygen cost per meter is modeled

The oxygen rate while walking, as our model computes it, shown here for no carried load. The terms in the bracket are in ml of oxygen per kg of body mass per minute, and the factor 0.1144 converts them to grams per minute for an 80 kg astronaut. The last term is the suit leakage that the Apollo suit specification allowed (NASA TN D-7883). The background is a view of the scene in our app.

To estimate oxygen consumption step by step, the model combines four empirical components plus a safety buffer:

  1. Level walking: Derived from NASA suited treadmill tests under simulated Mars gravity (Norcross et al., 2009, 2010). Limitation: based on 6 subjects in a single prototype suit on a flat surface.
  2. Terrain resistance: Adapted from Earth terrain multipliers (Pandolf et al., 1977) mapped to our four Mars surface types. Limitation: derived from unsuited walkers on Earth.
  3. Carried load: Modeled using the same NASA suited tests as added suit mass. Limitation: accounts for total weight, not how the load is distributed.
  4. Slope climb: Scaled from Earth incline walking data (Minetti et al., 2002) to suited Mars weight. Limitation: only validated up to a 0.45 grade (24°).
  5. Safety band: An extra 4 ml/kg/min (one standard deviation from the suit test fit) is added to every turn-back calculation.

To calculate the probability of finishing the plan, the app runs 1,000 simulated walks, stretching remaining travel and station times using historical Apollo delay distributions and scaling oxygen burn by historical Apollo used-to-planned ratios.

7. Checked against measured data

We validated the key components of our model against real measurements. Three tests failed, and each failure directly shaped how we bound the app's claims.

Checks that held up

  • Terrain classification: Tested against 322 held-out Curiosity images, our vision model achieved a mean overlap score of 0.69 (95% CI: 0.66–0.74) with human labels, performing strongly on soil (0.92), sand (0.87), and bedrock (0.82), though poorly on big rocks (0.18).
  • Solar position: Our computed sun angles match three Curiosity Mastcam image labels within 0.11°.
  • Route planner: The pathfinding algorithm passed all 30 test cases with known correct answers.
  • Steep-ground rule effectiveness: Across return paths simulated from 5,141 starting points, straight-line routes crossed steep ground 81% of the time and pure lowest-oxygen routes crossed it 66% of the time, whereas our rule reduced steep crossings to 22%. This safety margin costs a median of just 0.3% extra oxygen (though it can add 24% or more in the worst 10% of locations).

Checks that failed, and how we responded

  • Orbital slope overestimation: Across 61 Curiosity stops, the 1 m orbital elevation model read 7.2° steeper on average than the rover's onboard tilt sensor. Impact: Our steep-ground mask likely flags too much terrain, making estimated times and oxygen costs overly conservative. The app does not correct for this bias yet.
  • Orbital terrain classification: Predicting surface types from orbital data alone matched ground-camera labels only 38% of the time (worse than simply guessing the most common class at 52%). Response: Beyond the Navcam coverage zone, the display shows no terrain predictions and explicitly labels the ground as "assumed rocky."
  • Near-Earth storm forecasting: Feeding GOES-16 proton data from near Earth into a published Mars transfer model (Guo et al., 2020, preprint) matched Curiosity's readings within 1.0x to 2.7x for one storm, but underestimated two others by 49x to 463x. Response: We ruled out remote forecasting and keep the storm alarm tied exclusively to local ground readings.

Historical baseline data

Chart showing how Apollo astronauts often consumed more oxygen than planned.

  • Apollo oxygen variance: In 9 of 12 Apollo EVA records, astronauts used more oxygen than planned, and one crewmate required up to 1.22x the oxygen of their partner. Our 1,000-walk Monte Carlo simulation draws from these empirical distributions.

Curiosity's radiation measurements during the 20 May 2024 particle storm, showing when the alarm triggers. It provides 53 minutes of warning from the start of the first elevated reading, or 37 minutes once that 16-minute integration window completes.

8. Limitations

Because this is a research prototype and simulation, users should keep several constraints in mind:

  • Browser-based, not a physical headset: The interface runs in a desktop browser using keyboard navigation, simulated clocks, and simulated oxygen supplies.
  • Cross-planetary assumptions: Completion probabilities apply Apollo lunar variance data to Mars surface walks. While individual oxygen sub-models are grounded in published tests, the combined model has not been tested against a full suited Mars walk.
  • Heuristic thresholds: The 90% completion threshold, shadow avoidance penalty, and 10 m off-route trigger are engineering choices rather than empirically derived standards.
  • Spatial and grid limits: High-resolution terrain classification only covers two 48 m patches (and frequently misses large rocks), while the 8-direction movement grid can overestimate path lengths by up to 8%.
  • Reactive radiation alerts: The system detects rising radiation locally. It cannot forecast storms before they arrive.
  • Synthetic visuals: The sky, ground textures, and small scatter rocks are procedurally generated.

Every on-screen element, along with its exact data source and known limitations, is documented in docs/methods.md in the repository.

9. Try it yourself

  1. Launch: Open the demo link in a desktop browser to view the overview screen.
    • W to walk manually | P to toggle autonomous walking
    • T to advance the clock by 30 minutes
    • E to increase the partner's oxygen burn rate
    • R to replay the 20 May 2024 solar particle storm
    • C to toggle terrain-type overlays | M to open the overview map

10. Built with

  • Frontend: Three.js, Vite, and vanilla JavaScript
  • Data pipeline: Python
  • The use of AI/SI has been fully disclosed in the repository.
